article.para: Computers deal with text in several formats: programming-language code like C or C++, file formats like HTML, XML, JSON, and even user input such as with a text shell. These formats don't always use the same representations of the structures and values as the computer, however. For example, a JSON object might list a 7-digit number, like 5749175 as the series of digits 5749175, but a computer processing the data might represent that number internally as four bytes with the values 0, 87, 185, and 183. In this way, a representation is distinct from its actual value, much like how the number six can be represented as the word six, the Roman numeral VI, or the Arabic numeral 6.

Parsing is the process of processing the textual representation of data, and converting it to a form the computer can more easily work with. A JSON parser might convert JSON objects to a programming language’s internal structure types. An XML parser can convert an XML document to a tree structure that represents how the various elements in the document are organized. Siliko includes a parser that converts a mathematical notation that’s closer to one used by people than what a computer might use into a tree structure that’s easier for a computer to process.

section.title: Lexical Analysis
section.para: When parsing, there are two major steps. The first step is lexical analysis. This step involves the conversion of strings of arbitrary characters to usable units. For example, the string 40+7*11*5+12*3 could represent a series of numbers with a symbol between each adjacent pair of numbers, but to the computer, it’s 14 bytes, with the values 52 (4), 48 (0), 43 (+), 55 (7), 42 (*), 49 (1), 49 (1), 42 (*), 53 (5), 43 (+), 49 (1), 50 (2), 42 (*), and 51 (3). To make this series of bytes useful as the sequence number:40, symbol:+, number:7, symbol:*, number:11, symbol:*, number:5, symbol:+, number:12, symbol:*, and number:3, a tool called a lexical analyzer determines where the different pieces begin and where they end, and what type they are, then converts what it finds into a data structure called a token. Strictly speaking, the series of bytes to be converted for each piece is called a lexeme, and the data structure is called a token, but many programmers also refer to lexemes as tokens. Because lexical analysis converts lexemes to tokens, the process is also called tokenization, and a lexical analyzer can also be called a tokenizer. Another common name, used in the source code for Siliko Core for a lexical analyzer is lexer.

A lexical analyzer works by reading input one character at a time, whittling down the possible results as it reads each character until, by its internal rules, it has reached the end of input and narrowed down the possible type of the input to one type. This is done with a tool called a finite-state machine.

A finite-state machine has a set of states representing the possibilities and how far into the process it is. In the Siliko language integers and real numbers both start out with a series of digits, but real numbers also have a decimal point. So, when the lexical analyzer starts processing a new number, for example 12.5 it starts out in a ‘blank’ start state. It then reads the first character, 1. This puts the tokenizer into a state representing “maybe an integer”. It will then read the 2, and continue in the same state. When the analyzer reaches the decimal point, however, it knows that this isn’t an integer but rather a real number. So, it changes state to “real number”. Reading the next character, 5, the lexical analyzer continues in the “real number” state. It then reads the next character, which, presumably is an operator or a space character, and determines that the lexeme is done, and changes to a termination state. Once it has reached a termination state, the lexical analyzer does the final conversion to a useful form, a token representing the type of the data the lexeme represents in the language, in this case a real number, and the value itself in a more convenient form, such as the machine’s internal floating-point representation. The Lexical analyzer then passes this token on to the syntactic analyzer.

section.title: Syntactic Analysis
section.para: Syntactic analysis is the process of reading a series of tokens, provided by the lexical analyser, and converting them to a usable structure, most often a syntax tree. The tool that does this could be called a syntactic analyzer but is often simply called the parser.

This section of the parser takes care of making sense of what the arrangement of the tokens means. For example, an infix parser would look at a sequence of tokens such as number:40, symbol:+, number:7, symbol:*, number:11, symbol:*, number:5, symbol:+, number:12, symbol:*, and number:3, and concludes that such a sequence is a series of two addition operations, with number:40, and two series of multiplication operations, as operands. It would also determine the operands of the multiplication operations. It will then generate a syntax tree representing the operations.

A parser takes small bits of information, such as characters, and builds them into structures. It can then build a larger structure with the smaller structures. Ultimately, a parser will make a structure representing the totality of its input, such as the complete expression passed to Siliko or the entire JSON object passed to a JSON parser. These rules are called productions and the complete list of productions is called a grammar. The set of valid inputs that a grammar describes is called a language. Programming languages are one form of such a language, but notations like JSON, and formats like XML are also languages.

note.para: Extended Backus-Naur Form is standardized as ISO standard 14977, but no one follows the ISO standard, not even ISO. There are several different specifications of EBNF each trying to resolve problems with the original Backus-Naur Form, and there is no clear de facto standard. This manual uses a version used by the World Wide Web Consortium, in the Notation section of the XML Recommendation.

section.para: A simple example of a production is [0-9]+, written using regular expression notation to simplify the rules. Each production is identified by a name. This name, and the text the production represents are called a nonterminal. A terminal is a literal character such as '+'.
There are three special properties of the productions for the expression and term nonterminals to notice.

The first is they can each have themselves as components. So, given the expression 2 + 3 + 5 the first expression 2 + 3 is a component of a second expression which has (2 + 3), +, and 5 as its component.

The second is that these productions can match text that is just the next production; an expression can match a simple term, and a term can match a simple number. This means that an expression can match a simple number.

The third is that these productions use themselves as one operand to their operation, and the next nonterminal as the other. This helps facilitate processing with precedence or an order of operations. Because the multiplication is a deeper rule than addition, it has to be processed first, and forms a branch on the parse tree for the operation.
For the complete grammar of the Siliko infix language, see the Formal Grammar section of the Siliko Infix Language Reference.
